soteriology.summary: Christians agree that people are saved by God's grace through Jesus. They disagree about how God's choice and our choice fit together. Some say God alone decides who will believe, others say God makes faith possible for everyone and people can accept or refuse. Several traditions sit in between or frame the question differently.
soteriology.takeaway: The real question is whether God's grace decides the outcome by itself or makes a free human response possible.
soteriology.whyItMatters: It shapes how people pray for friends who do not believe, how preachers make an appeal, and where believers find assurance. It also affects how Christians talk about God's fairness and love when someone never comes to faith.

calvinism.summary: Calvinists believe sin has left people unable to turn to God on their own. So before the world began God chose, out of pure mercy, to save particular people, and he makes sure each of them comes to faith. Salvation is from start to finish God's work, which is meant to bring deep humility and security.
calvinism.takeaway: Salvation rests entirely on God's choice, so he gets all the credit and his people cannot be lost.
calvinism.analogy: Like a rescuer who pulls an unconscious swimmer from the sea, the saved person does not help with their own rescue at all.

arminianism.summary: Arminians agree people cannot turn to God unaided, but believe God gives enabling grace (sometimes called 'prevenient' grace, meaning grace that comes first) to everyone who hears the gospel. That grace frees people to believe, yet it can be resisted. God chose to save all who would trust in Christ, and he truly wants every person to be saved.
arminianism.takeaway: God makes faith possible for everyone, and each person can welcome or refuse his grace.
arminianism.analogy: Like a doctor who gives every patient the medicine that lets them stand up, but leaves each one free to take it or not.

molinism.summary: Molinists believe God knows not only what will happen but what every person would freely do in any possible situation (called 'middle knowledge'). Using that knowledge, God chose to create a world where his purposes are fully achieved through people's genuinely free choices. This lets them hold strong views of both God's control and human freedom.
molinism.takeaway: God steers history perfectly by knowing in advance how free people would choose in every circumstance.
molinism.analogy: Like an author who knows each character so well that he can set up scenes where they freely do exactly what the story needs.

provisionism.summary: Provisionists, many of them Southern Baptists, believe Christ died for every person and the gospel message itself, powered by the Holy Spirit, is enough to let anyone respond. People are affected by sin but are not so ruined that they cannot hear and believe when God speaks. Election means God chose to save those who are 'in Christ' by faith.
provisionism.takeaway: God has provided salvation for everyone, and the gospel itself gives every hearer a real chance to respond.
provisionism.analogy: Like a pardon offered to every prisoner, written so plainly that anyone who reads it can accept it.

lutheran.summary: Lutherans teach that salvation is wholly God's gift: the sinful will cannot cooperate, and God chose his people for salvation in Christ. But they deny that God chose anyone for damnation; those who are lost resist grace by their own fault. They hold both truths together without a system to reconcile them, pointing anxious people to their baptism and the promises of the gospel.
lutheran.takeaway: If you are saved it is all God's doing, and if you are lost it is all your own fault, and the gap is left as a mystery.
lutheran.analogy: Like a gift placed in your hands that you did nothing to earn, while the only way to miss it is to throw it away.

eastern-orthodox.summary: The Orthodox see salvation as healing and union with God (called 'theosis', meaning sharing in God's life), not mainly a legal verdict. God always takes the lead, but people respond and cooperate with his grace over a lifetime, which they call 'synergy' (working together). They generally avoid the Western argument about predestination altogether.
eastern-orthodox.takeaway: Salvation is a lifelong healing in which God's grace and our free response work together.
eastern-orthodox.analogy: Like a patient in a hospital who is healed by the doctor's care, yet must keep taking part in the treatment day by day.

cessationism.summary: The New Testament describes gifts like prophecy, speaking in tongues and miraculous healing. Christians disagree about whether God still gives these gifts today in the same way. Some believe they stopped after the apostles, some believe they continue, and some sit in between.
cessationism.takeaway: The question is whether the miraculous gifts were a one-time sign for the founding of the church or a normal part of church life in every age.
cessationism.whyItMatters: It affects whether churches pray for healing expecting miracles, whether they welcome prophecy or tongues in worship, and how people test claims that 'God told me'. It also shapes how believers understand the Bible's authority alongside present-day experience.

cessationism.summary: Cessationists believe the miraculous 'sign' gifts, such as new prophecy, tongues and healing gifts, were given to confirm the apostles' message while the New Testament was being written. Once Scripture was complete, those gifts ended, though God still answers prayer and can do miracles as he chooses. This guards the Bible as the final word from God.
cessationism.takeaway: The miraculous gifts were the scaffolding for the early church, and the finished Bible now stands in their place.
cessationism.analogy: Like the signed certificate that confirms a new building is sound, which is not reissued every time someone walks through the door.

continuationism.summary: Continuationists believe every gift of the Spirit listed in the New Testament, including prophecy, tongues and healing, is still available today. Nothing in the Bible says they would stop before Jesus returns, and the church still needs them. They usually teach that modern prophecy must be tested and is never equal to Scripture.
continuationism.takeaway: The Spirit who gave gifts to the first Christians gives the same gifts to Christians now.
continuationism.analogy: Like a toolbox handed to the whole church that is meant to stay in use until the job is finished.

open-but-cautious.summary: This view says the Bible does not teach that the miraculous gifts have ended, so Christians should stay open to them. But people in this camp are wary of hype, unchecked claims and practices they think go beyond Scripture. They welcome the gifts in principle while testing everything carefully.
open-but-cautious.takeaway: Stay open to the miraculous gifts, but test every claim with care.
open-but-cautious.analogy: Like leaving the front door unlocked for a friend you expect, while still checking who is actually knocking.

gender-roles.summary: All sides agree that men and women are equally made in God's image and equally loved. They disagree about whether God intends some roles in church leadership and marriage to belong to men. Catholic and Orthodox churches add a third angle based on what the priest represents in worship.
gender-roles.takeaway: The disagreement is whether equal worth comes with some different God-given roles, or with full equality of roles as well.
gender-roles.whyItMatters: It decides who can preach, lead churches and be ordained, and how couples understand leadership and decisions at home. It also affects how many women experience their calling and how churches read hard passages.

complementarianism.summary: Complementarians believe men and women are fully equal in value but were designed to complement each other, like two different parts that fit together. In marriage the husband is called to lead in loving, self-giving service, and in the church the office of pastor or elder is for qualified men. Women serve in many other vital ministries.
complementarianism.takeaway: Equal in worth, different in some God-given roles.
complementarianism.analogy: Like two players on the same team with equal value but different positions, each needed for the team to work.

egalitarianism.summary: Egalitarians believe the Bible, read as a whole and in its historical setting, teaches equality of roles as well as worth. Any gifted and called person, man or woman, may lead, preach and pastor, and marriage is a partnership of mutual submission. The passages that limit women are read as answers to local problems, not rules for all time.
egalitarianism.takeaway: Equal in worth and equally free to serve in any role God calls them to.
egalitarianism.analogy: Like a team where positions are given by skill and calling, not by who happens to be a man or a woman.

sacramental.summary: Catholic and Orthodox churches ordain only men as priests and bishops, but mainly for a reason tied to worship rather than to men ruling women. The priest acts 'in the person of Christ' at the altar, and Jesus chose men as his apostles, which the church believes it has no authority to change. Women are honoured in many roles, with Mary the highest of all the saints.
sacramental.takeaway: The male priesthood is about representing Christ in the sacraments, not about men being in charge.
sacramental.analogy: Like an actor cast to portray a particular historical person, where the role is not a claim to be better than the rest of the cast.

atonement.summary: Every Christian tradition says Jesus' death and resurrection save us. They differ on how, and over the centuries people have used different pictures: a victory, a payment, a debt of honour, a display of love, a healing. Many Christians think several pictures are true together, but they argue about which one is central.
atonement.takeaway: The debate is about what exactly went wrong between us and God, and therefore what the cross had to do to fix it.
atonement.whyItMatters: It shapes how people talk about God's anger and love, how they understand guilt and forgiveness, and what they think victory over evil looks like. Preaching, worship songs and pastoral care all change depending on which picture leads.

recapitulation.summary: This early view, linked with Irenaeus in the 100s, says Jesus saves by living through every stage of human life and getting right everything Adam got wrong. He becomes a new head of the human race, so that those joined to him share his healed humanity. The cross is the climax of a whole life of obedience.
recapitulation.takeaway: Jesus redoes the human story faithfully, so we can start again in him.
recapitulation.analogy: Like a musician replaying a piece someone botched, note by note, so the whole song can finally be heard as it was written.

ransom.summary: The ransom view takes seriously Jesus' words that he came to give his life 'as a ransom for many'. People sold themselves into slavery to sin and the devil, and Christ's death is the price that buys them back. Early writers said the devil was tricked, because he could not hold the sinless Son of God in death.
ransom.takeaway: Jesus paid the price to free us from captivity to sin and the devil.
ransom.analogy: Like someone paying a kidnapper's demand to bring a captive home, only to find the kidnapper cannot keep the money.

christus-victor.summary: 'Christus Victor' means 'Christ the Victor'. Humanity is held captive by hostile powers such as sin, death and the devil, and on the cross and in the resurrection Jesus fights them and wins. Salvation is liberation, like being freed when a tyrant is overthrown.
christus-victor.takeaway: The cross and empty tomb are Jesus' victory over everything that enslaves us.
christus-victor.analogy: Like a champion who defeats the bully holding a whole town in fear, so everyone can walk free.

satisfaction.summary: Anselm, an archbishop in the 1000s, argued that sin dishonours God, and that justice requires the honour to be restored. Only humans owe that debt, but only God could pay it, so God became human in Jesus. His freely given death is worth more than all the debt, and its value is shared with sinners.
satisfaction.takeaway: Jesus, as God and man, repaid the debt of honour that we owed and could never cover.
satisfaction.analogy: Like a friend who covers an enormous debt you owe a king, paying with something worth far more than the debt itself.

moral-influence.summary: This view, linked with Peter Abelard, says the main way the cross saves is by changing our hearts. God was never unwilling to forgive; what needed fixing was our fear and coldness toward him. Seeing how far Jesus would go in love melts our hearts and draws us back to God.
moral-influence.takeaway: The cross saves by showing a love so great that it wins us back.
moral-influence.analogy: Like a parent whose patient, costly love finally wins over a runaway child more than any punishment could.

penal-substitution.summary: 'Penal substitution' means Jesus took the penalty for sin in our place. God is holy and just and cannot simply ignore wrongdoing, but in love he sent his Son to bear the punishment we deserved. Because Jesus carried it, God can forgive sinners and still be completely just.
penal-substitution.takeaway: Jesus took the punishment we deserved so that we could be forgiven.
penal-substitution.analogy: Like a judge who rightly sentences a guilty person and then steps down from the bench to serve the sentence himself.

governmental.summary: Developed by Hugo Grotius in the 1600s, this view sees God mainly as the wise ruler of the universe. To forgive sinners without making sin look harmless, God displayed on the cross how serious sin is. That public display upholds his moral order so that he can freely pardon those who repent.
governmental.takeaway: The cross shows how serious sin is, so God's pardon never makes wrongdoing seem trivial.
governmental.analogy: Like a ruler who grants an amnesty but first makes clear, at great personal cost, that the law still matters.

mimetic-scapegoat.summary: Based on René Girard's work, this view notices that human groups often settle their conflicts by blaming and killing an innocent 'scapegoat'. Jesus willingly became that victim, and the Gospels tell the story from the victim's side, exposing the lie behind such violence. The resurrection shows God siding with the victim and calls us out of the cycle of blame.
mimetic-scapegoat.takeaway: The cross unmasks our habit of blaming and killing the innocent, and invites us to stop.
mimetic-scapegoat.analogy: Like a video that finally shows a playground mob from the side of the kid they picked on, so nobody can pretend it was fair.

healing-participatory.summary: This view, strong in Eastern Orthodox churches, sees sin mainly as a sickness that corrupts human nature and leads to death. In Jesus, God took on our nature, carried it through death and raised it to new life, healing it from the inside. We are saved by being joined to him and sharing his life, a process called 'theosis'.
healing-participatory.takeaway: Jesus heals our broken human nature by joining it to God's own life.
healing-participatory.analogy: Like a healthy donor whose bone marrow, once shared, rebuilds a sick patient's blood from within.

hell.summary: Jesus warns often about judgment, and Christians agree that evil will be dealt with. They disagree about what final punishment is like and how long it lasts. The main views are never-ending punishment, final destruction, and eventual restoration of everyone.
hell.takeaway: The disagreement is whether the lost suffer forever, cease to exist, or are finally brought back to God.
hell.whyItMatters: It shapes how urgently people share their faith, how they speak about God's justice and mercy, and how they grieve for loved ones who did not believe. It also tests how believers read words like 'eternal' and 'destruction'.

eternal-conscious-torment.summary: This traditional view holds that those who reject God are raised and sent, body and soul, into punishment that is conscious and never ends. Sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious, and Jesus describes the punishment with the same word, 'eternal', that he uses for life. It has been the majority view through most of church history.
eternal-conscious-torment.takeaway: Final punishment is real, conscious and everlasting, just as eternal life is everlasting.
eternal-conscious-torment.analogy: Like a door that, once shut by the person's own final choice, stays shut forever.

conditional-immortality.summary: Also called 'annihilationism', this view says only God is naturally immortal, and endless life is a gift given in Christ. The unsaved are raised, judged and punished as their sins deserve, and then they are destroyed and cease to exist. The punishment is 'eternal' because its result can never be undone.
conditional-immortality.takeaway: The lost do not live forever in torment; they are finally destroyed.
conditional-immortality.analogy: Like a fire that burns until nothing is left, rather than one that burns the same log forever.

christian-universalism.summary: Christian universalists believe God will in the end bring every person to repentance and faith through Christ. Hell is real and can be long and severe, but its purpose is to purify and correct, not to punish without end. God's love will not be finally defeated in anyone.
christian-universalism.takeaway: Hell is real but temporary, because God's love will eventually win every person back.
christian-universalism.analogy: Like a refiner's fire that burns away the impurities until only the gold remains.

heaven-new-creation.summary: Christians agree that believers will be with God forever. They differ on where and how: is the goal a spiritual heaven where we see God, or a renewed physical earth with resurrected bodies? Many hold both, in two stages.
heaven-new-creation.takeaway: The question is whether the final hope is going to heaven or heaven coming down to a renewed earth.
heaven-new-creation.whyItMatters: It affects how Christians value the body, work, art and care for the earth, and how they comfort the grieving. It also shapes how people picture eternity, as rest and worship, or also as renewed life and work.

heaven-as-destination.summary: This view, strong in Catholic and classical theology, holds that the final goal of life is God himself, seen directly face to face (called the 'beatific vision', meaning the vision that brings perfect happiness). Believers go to be with God at death and are later raised bodily, but the heart of heaven is knowing and enjoying God. Everything else is secondary to that.
heaven-as-destination.takeaway: The greatest joy of eternity is seeing and enjoying God himself.
heaven-as-destination.analogy: Like finally meeting face to face the person whose letters you have treasured all your life.

new-creation.summary: This view stresses that the Christian hope is not escaping to heaven but bodily resurrection and the renewal of the whole world. Heaven and earth will be joined, and God will live among his people on a restored creation. Life will be physical, social and full of meaningful activity, without sin or death.
new-creation.takeaway: God will not throw creation away but make it new, and we will live there in resurrected bodies.
new-creation.analogy: Like a beloved old house that is fully restored, not demolished, so the family can move back in.

intermediate-and-final.summary: This view, found in many Protestant confessions, holds that Christian hope comes in two stages. At death believers' souls go straight to be with Christ in a conscious, blessed state, sometimes called the 'intermediate state'. Then at Jesus' return they are raised bodily to live forever in the new heavens and new earth.
intermediate-and-final.takeaway: First we go to be with Christ, then we come back with him to a renewed world.
intermediate-and-final.analogy: Like waiting happily in the host's living room before the full party begins in the newly finished garden.

christocentric-hermeneutic.summary: A 'hermeneutic' is simply a way of reading and interpreting. Christians agree Jesus is central to the Bible, but they disagree about how he should shape the reading of hard Old Testament passages, especially where God commands violence or judgment. Some read those passages through the cross, some take them as true pictures of God's justice, and some see a story building toward Christ.
christocentric-hermeneutic.takeaway: The question is whether Jesus corrects, confirms, or completes the Old Testament's portraits of God.
christocentric-hermeneutic.whyItMatters: It shapes how people teach difficult stories, how they speak about God's justice and anger, and how they answer critics of the Bible. It also affects how Christians think about violence, nonviolence and judgment today.

christocentric-cruciform.summary: 'Cruciform' means cross-shaped. This view holds that Jesus, especially the crucified Jesus, is the clearest and final picture of what God is like. All Scripture is inspired, but Old Testament portraits of God commanding violence are read through the cross, sometimes as God stooping to his people's limited understanding.
christocentric-cruciform.takeaway: If you want to know what God is like, look first at Jesus on the cross and read the rest in that light.
christocentric-cruciform.analogy: Like judging old blurry photos of someone by the clear, live video you now have of them.

flat-canonical.summary: This view holds that every part of the Bible truly shows God's character, even if some parts show it more fully than others. The God who brought judgment on the Canaanites is the same God revealed in Jesus, who also speaks of judgment. Divine judgment is seen as just and holy, not as a misunderstanding to be corrected.
flat-canonical.takeaway: The same just and loving God is shown truly in every part of Scripture, including its judgments.
flat-canonical.analogy: Like a good judge who is both kind at home and firm in court, with both sides being his real character.

christotelic-progressive-revelation.summary: 'Christotelic' means 'aimed at Christ as the goal'. This view sees the Bible as one story moving forward toward Jesus, who fulfils and reshapes what came before. The Old Testament is read again in his light, but its original meaning in its own time is still respected rather than overruled.
christotelic-progressive-revelation.takeaway: The whole Bible is a story heading toward Jesus, who brings its earlier parts to their full meaning.
christotelic-progressive-revelation.analogy: Like a mystery novel whose earlier chapters make full sense only once you reach the ending.
